title: Auditing Fundamentals
summary: Learn how audits work: external and internal audit, materiality and the audit risk model, internal controls, evidence and sampling, fraud, ethics and independence, and the types of audit opinion.
audience: Accounting and finance students, junior auditors, managers and board members

body.p: An audit is an independent examination of information to give users confidence in it. An external audit of financial statements leads to an opinion on whether they give a true and fair view (or are fairly presented) in accordance with the applicable financial reporting framework, such as IFRS. Shareholders, lenders, tax authorities and regulators rely on that opinion.

list: External audit: by independent registered auditors, often required by company law.
Internal audit: by the organisation's own team (or an outsourced one), reviewing risk management, controls and governance, and reporting to the audit committee.
Public-sector audit: by supreme audit institutions such as the Auditor-General, checking how public money is used.
Other assurance: reviews, agreed-upon procedures, and assurance on sustainability or IT systems.

body.p: External auditors follow International Standards on Auditing (ISAs) and ethical codes. An audit gives reasonable assurance, a high but not absolute level, because it relies on testing samples and on judgement.

body.tip: Remember that management prepares the financial statements; the auditor gives an opinion on them.

body.p: Auditors cannot check everything, so they focus on areas where material misstatements are most likely.

A misstatement is material if it could reasonably influence users' decisions. Auditors set an overall materiality, often using a benchmark such as about 5% of profit before tax. For a company with profit before tax of R2 000 000, materiality might be around R100 000. A lower performance materiality (for example 75%, R75 000) is used for testing to allow for undetected errors.

Audit risk = inherent risk x control risk x detection risk. Inherent and control risk are assessed (the risk of material misstatement); detection risk is what the auditor controls through the amount of testing. If acceptable audit risk is 5%, inherent risk is assessed at 60% and control risk at 50%, then detection risk can be at most 0.05 / (0.6 x 0.5), about 16.7%, so substantial testing is needed.

list: Higher-risk areas include revenue recognition, estimates, related-party transactions and cash.
Understanding the business, its industry and its controls comes first.
Risks of fraud must always be considered.

body.tip: The higher the assessed risk, the more and better evidence you need.

body.p: Internal controls are the policies and procedures an organisation uses to protect assets, produce reliable records and comply with laws. Strong controls reduce errors and fraud; auditors test them to decide how much they can rely on them.

list: Segregation of duties: no single person should authorise, record and have custody of the same transaction. The person who approves payments should not also enter them and reconcile the bank account.
Authorisation limits: purchases above set amounts need senior approval.
Physical controls: locked stores, safes, access cards and stock counts.
Reconciliations: bank, debtors and creditors reconciled regularly and reviewed.
IT controls: user access rights, passwords, change management and backups.
Documentation: pre-numbered documents, so missing items are noticed.

body.p: Controls work only within a good "tone at the top": leaders who act with integrity, an active audit committee and clear accountability. Small organisations with few staff often lack segregation of duties, so owner oversight and review become more important.

body.tip: When you design a process, ask: "How could someone steal or make an error here without being noticed?" Then add a control.

body.p: Auditors gather sufficient, appropriate evidence. Evidence is more reliable when it comes from independent outside sources, is obtained directly by the auditor, and is documented rather than oral.

list: Inspection of documents and physical assets.
Observation, for example of a stock count.
Inquiry of management and staff (never enough on its own).
External confirmation, such as bank and customer confirmations.
Recalculation and reperformance.
Analytical procedures: comparing figures with expectations, prior years or industry ratios to spot unusual changes.

body.p: With thousands of transactions, auditors test samples. In systematic or monetary-unit sampling, a R1 000 000 population tested with 50 items gives an interval of R20 000: every 20 000th rand is selected, so larger items are more likely to be chosen. If 3 errors are found in a sample of 60 invoices (5%), the auditor projects the error rate to the population: 5% of 12 000 invoices suggests about 600 may contain errors, then decides whether further work is needed.

body.tip: Document every test: what was done, by whom, the results and the conclusion. If it is not documented, it was not done.

body.p: Fraud is intentional deception for gain: stealing assets (such as cash, stock or fake suppliers) or manipulating financial statements (such as inflating revenue). The fraud triangle explains why it happens: pressure (debts, targets), opportunity (weak controls) and rationalisation ("I'll pay it back").

list: Staff who never take leave or refuse to share duties.
Unusual journal entries, especially near the year-end.
Suppliers with addresses matching employees, or many round-sum payments.
Lifestyles beyond known income.
Missing documents and unexplained differences in reconciliations.

body.p: Auditors follow ethical codes such as the IESBA Code: integrity, objectivity, professional competence and due care, confidentiality and professional behaviour. Independence is vital: auditors must avoid financial interests in clients, close family or business relationships, and providing services that would mean auditing their own work. Professional scepticism means questioning evidence rather than accepting management's explanations at face value.

body.tip: If something feels wrong, ask for evidence. Polite scepticism protects you, the client's stakeholders and the profession.

body.p: At the end of the audit, the auditor evaluates uncorrected misstatements and evidence, then issues a report.

list: Unmodified (clean): the statements are fairly presented in all material respects.
Qualified: fairly presented except for a specific material matter, either a misstatement or limited evidence, that is not pervasive.
Adverse: material misstatements are pervasive; the statements are not fairly presented.
Disclaimer of opinion: the auditor could not obtain enough evidence, and the possible effects are material and pervasive.

body.p: Reports of listed companies also describe key audit matters, the areas of most significance in the audit. Separate paragraphs may draw attention to matters such as material uncertainty about the business continuing as a going concern.

Auditors also report control weaknesses to management and those charged with governance, with recommendations. Acting on these management letters strengthens the organisation and often makes the next audit smoother.

body.tip: Read the audit report before relying on any company's financial statements, especially the opinion paragraph and any going-concern comments.

quiz.q: What does an external audit opinion address?
options: Whether the company will be profitable
Whether the financial statements are fairly presented

quiz.q: Profit before tax R2 000 000 with materiality at 5% gives:
Audit risk 5%, inherent risk 60%, control risk 50%. Maximum detection risk is about:
High assessed risk means the auditor should:

options: No one person authorises, records and holds custody of a transaction

quiz.q: Which is the most reliable evidence?
options: An oral explanation from a junior employee
A confirmation received directly from the customer's bank

quiz.q: A R1 000 000 population tested with 50 items gives a sampling interval of:
3 errors in a sample of 60 invoices projected to 12 000 invoices suggests about:
The three parts of the fraud triangle are:

options: Owning shares in the audit client
Fairly presented except for a specific material, non-pervasive matter
Questioning evidence instead of accepting explanations at face value
